title: Long-term comparative analysis of AAV9-mediated gene replacement therapies for spinal muscular atrophy in mice
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 23 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-73545-8

In mice, a next-generation gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy improved survival and motor function more than a Zolgensma-like treatment, with fewer signs of liver and heart toxicity, supporting its promise as a safer, more effective approach.
headline: New gene therapy for muscle-wasting disease works better and safer than existing treatment in mice.
why_it_matters: Spinal muscular atrophy is a genetic disease that causes progressive muscle weakness and can be fatal. This research shows a promising new approach that could help patients live longer and move better while causing less damage to vital organs like the liver and heart.
key_findings: A next-generation gene therapy (using AAV9, a modified virus that delivers healthy genes into cells) improved survival and motor function (ability to move and control muscles) better than Zolgensma, an existing approved gene therapy for this disease.
The new therapy caused fewer signs of liver toxicity (damage to the liver) and heart toxicity (damage to the heart) compared to the current standard treatment.
Long-term testing in mice showed sustained benefits, meaning the therapy continued to work over extended periods rather than losing effectiveness over time.
The improved safety profile suggests the new approach could translate to fewer side effects in human patients, though this still needs to be tested in clinical trials (studies in humans).
methods_snapshot: Researchers compared two gene therapy approaches in mice with spinal muscular atrophy, measuring survival, muscle function, and organ damage over an extended period. They used standard laboratory assessments and genetic analysis to track how well each therapy worked and what side effects occurred.

glossary.definition: A harmless virus engineered to carry healthy genes into cells, acting like a delivery truck for genetic medicine.
Treatment that introduces a healthy copy of a faulty gene into a patient's cells to fix the underlying genetic problem.
A genetic disease where nerve cells die, causing progressive weakness and loss of muscle control, often starting in infancy or childhood.
The first approved gene therapy treatment for spinal muscular atrophy, used as a benchmark to compare against the new therapy.
The ability of muscles to contract and move the body, including walking, grasping, and other physical activities.
Damage or poisoning caused by a treatment or substance in specific organs or tissues.

limitations: This study was conducted in mice, which don't always respond to treatments the same way humans do—so the results must be confirmed in human clinical trials before this therapy can be widely used. The long-term safety in humans over years or decades remains unknown.
